Vināyakaśānti
------------------------------------------
Sometimes called Gaṇapatipūjā, this śānti (propitiatory rite) is generally performed at the commencement of all सṁस्कारस् or sacraments like उपनयन, विवाह (marriage), as also for averting the evil effects of स्तर्स् and प्लनेत्स्, and so on.
When it is performed independently, śuklapakṣa-caturthī (4th day of the bright fortnight) associated with auspicious स्तर्स् like पुष्य, Śrāvaṇa, रोहिणी and अश्विनी as also the weekday, Thursday, is recommended.
The Bhaviṣyottarapurāṇa (

) gives a Gaṇapatiśānti, which is similar to the विनायकशान्ति.
See also ŚĀNTIS.

Vindhya
------------------------------------------
This is the famous mountain range separating the Deccan Plateau from the Indo-Gangetic plains of North India.
According to the ancient legends, the विन्ध्य mountain (considered a living deity) asked सूर्य (the Sun-god) to circumambulate him also, even as he was doing to the मेरु mountain. When सूर्य politely refused, विन्ध्य started growing taller and taller, obstructing his path. The gods in हेअवेन् who were alarmed at this, requested the great sage अगस्त्य to intervene. When अगस्त्य arrived, विन्ध्य bowed down to him. The sage commanded him to be like that, until he returned from the south, which he never did!
Some of the rivers that take their birth from the विन्ध्य are: Tapatī, Payoṣṇī, Nirvindhyā, Veṇā, Kumudvatī, Durgamā and Śīlā.
Vindhyapṛṣṭha is the territory of this region wherein the following races (of people) live: Mālada, Karuṣa, Utkala, Māṣa, Daśārṇa, भोज, Kiṣkindhaka, Vītihotra and अवन्ति (vide Matsyapurāṇa

Vināyaka
(‘one who has no master’)
------------------------------------------
See GAṆAPATI.
This word is sometimes used to indicate बुद्ध and गरुड also.
In the Mānavagṛhyasūtras (2.14) four Vināyakas have been mentioned. They are: Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa, Kūṣmāṇḍarājaputra, Usmita and Devayajana.
These Vināyakas are evil spirits causing such obstacles in life as maidens not getting good husbands, married ladies not blessed with children, princes not becoming kings though eligible, men losing one’s children or crops and so on. Propitiatory rites like विनायकशान्ति or Gaṇapatipūjā have to be done to offset these evil spirits.

viniyogavidhi
(‘injunction regarding application’)
------------------------------------------
Vedic sacrifices involve quite complicated rites. Hence treatises on the Pūrva-mīmāṁsā take great pains to explain in detail all the subtle points in their performance.
A विधि is a Vedic injunction regarding the performance of any Vedic rite like a याग or sacrifice.
Some of the vidhis are: utpattividhi or pradhānavidhi; विनियोगविधि or गुण-विधि; viśiṣṭavidhi.
The first विधि indicates the main rite such as, ‘One who desires to attain स्वर्ग (heaven) should perform the अग्निहोत्र sacrifice.’
The second one, the विनियोगविधि, gives the details of the performance, like ‘He has to offer curds as oblation into the fire (of अग्निहोत्र).’
In the third one, the viśiṣṭavidhi, the speciality is pointed out. For instance, if it is declared, ‘One has to perform the sacrifice through सोम,’ it should be understood that a sacrifice in which the सोम juice is to be offered, is meant here.

Vinatā
------------------------------------------
She was a daughter of Dakṣaprajāpatī and one of the 13 wives of the sage कश्यप. अरुण, the charioteer of सूर्य (Sun-god) and गरुड (the eagle-mount of विष्णु) were her sons.
Since her pregnancy had lasted too long, she is said to have pressed her belly. As a result, the baby inside (i.e. अरुण) was deformed. He was born without the thighs. Hence he was named ‘Anūru’ (one without thighs).
Once she lost a bet with her co-wife कद्रू and had to become her slave. गरुड released her from स्लवेर्य् by getting कद्रू what she wanted.

Vinaśana
------------------------------------------
Sarasvatī, the mighty river of ऋग्वेद fame—called nadītamā in the Ṛgveda (2.41.16)—now known as Sarsuti, comes down the Siwalik range near Ambala (in the Haryana State) and disappears in the sands near Sirsa. This place was called विनशन during the period of the Mahābhārata (vide Araṇyaparva 130.2).
According to the Manusmṛti (2.21) it was the western limit of what was then known as the मध्यदेश.
